Population.evidence_source: The aim of this paper is to examine weeks prior to completed suicide, particularly in relation to key events in the weeks leading up to the death, from the perspectives of immediate family survivors.

Area.evidence_source: Distress can be exacerbated because of the unexpected nature of suicide, meaning survivors may not have anticipated the loss, and the consequent stigma, as well as disruptions and stress to the family system (Cvinar, 2005). Thus suicide survivors are left to contemplate the death and reflect on events leading up to the death, and consider the reasons why. Indeed, in the aftermath, survivors are left with many unanswered questions (Fielden, 2003). There may be a sense of failing the decedent and a sense that significant cues were missed that could have indicated an imminent suicide and possibly changed the outcome. Suicide survivorship is widely understood as being confusing, traumatic, deeply disturbing, and carrying considerable health burden (Fielden, 2003; Mitchell et al., 2004), with survivors themselves a known high-risk group for mental health problems, including suicidality (Cerel & Campbell, 2008). Furthermore, there is evidence that suicide survivorship is associated with isolation, withdrawal, stigmatisation, and negative social judgment (Cvinar, 2005). The propensity for feelings of regret, shame, rejection, stigma, guilt, and self-blame in suicide survivors is known (Cvinar, 2005; Fielden, 2003; Mitchell et al., 2004)
